section_summary: This section consists of U.S. Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI) reports, attach\u00e9 summaries, and State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs analytical memoranda dating primarily from March 1932 to March 1933 (with an isolated 1928 naval aviation report). The documents trace the escalating dominance of the Japanese military over civil cabinets, the consolidation of Manchuria and Manchukuo, border frictions around Shanhaikwan and the Soviet frontier, and growing ideological extremism and domestic fascism. They also examine diplomatic confrontations at the League of Nations over the Lytton Report, Japanese-American strategic tensions in the Pacific and Hawaii, constitutional clashes over the Emperor's Supreme Command prerogative, and Japan's worsening financial strain and industrial reorganization.

subfiles.about: An attach\u00e9 report recording the experimental sinking of the decommissioned destroyer Hatsuharu by naval aircraft in Tokyo Bay.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The decommissioned destroyer Hatsuharu was sunk by aerial bombing in the open sea off Tokyo Bay on August 18, 1928, after being towed by the cruiser Kasuga. Aircraft from the aircraft carriers Akagi and Hosho, the seaplane tender Notoro, and the Oppama Air Station dropped bombs from altitudes between 1,000 and 3,000 meters, descending to lower altitudes to deliver the final hits. The Combined Fleet assembled to observe the exercise, attended by the Minister of the Navy and senior naval officers.
subfiles.title: ONI Attach\u00e9 Report: Old Destroyer Hatsuharu Sunk by Airplane Bombs
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department

subfiles.about: A confidential ONI memorandum relaying a Tokyo dispatch that forecasts a new national cabinet under Privy Councillor Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.summary: The Office of Naval Intelligence forwards a confidential dispatch received from the Naval Attach\u00e9 in Tokyo. The dispatch predicts that following the adjournment of the Diet's special session, a new national unity cabinet headed by Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma of the Privy Council is likely to be formed. It adds that replacing the current Minister of War in such a transition is not expected to cause any loss of military prestige.
subfiles.title: ONI Memorandum: Confidential Dispatch on Prospective Cabinet Headed by Baron Hiranuma
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A War Department routing slip transmitting an intelligence report on Japan to the State Department Far Eastern Division.
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, War Department
subfiles.summary: A standard Military Intelligence Division routing sheet circulating an intelligence report concerning Japan. The document indicates distribution to various military branches and routes the file to the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs for information and filing.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Routing Slip to Far Eastern Division
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An ONI transmittal memorandum requesting that an attached report on Japan be forwarded to the State Department.
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.summary: The Office of Naval Intelligence directs a memorandum to Major Crane of the Military Intelligence Division, War Department. It requests that the attached intelligence report on Japan be forwarded to the Far Eastern Division of the State Department once the War Department has finished reviewing it.
subfiles.title: ONI Memorandum for Major Crane on Transmittal of Japan Report
subfiles.to: Major Crane, Military Intelligence Division, War Department

subfiles.about: An intelligence report analyzing upcoming Diet legislation, the controversy over the South Manchuria Railway presidency, rising fascist organizations, and White Russian activities.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The report previews the special Diet session scheduled for May 1932, discussing supplementary budgets, currency inflation, and expected opposition attacks regarding Manchuria and Shanghai. It chronicles the political confrontation between Premier Inukai's Seiyukai government and the Army over the attempted replacement of South Manchuria Railway president Count Yasuya Uchida, which ended in total capitulation by Inukai. It also traces the growth of Japanese fascist and right-wing groups emerging from splits in the Social Democratic and Japan Mass parties under figures like Kenzo Adachi and Seigo Nakano, and reports on meetings in Kobe between White Russian ataman General Semyonov, War Minister Araki, and Railways Minister Tokonami.
subfiles.title: ONI Report No. 8: Comments on the Political Situation
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department analytical memorandum summarizing ONI Report No. 153 and evaluating three translated articles on military thought and Pacific strategy.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury summarizes Tokyo ONI Report No. 153 and its three translated enclosures. The first enclosure is an unabridged translation of War Minister Sadao Araki's widely read nationalist pamphlet outlining his 'back to Asia' doctrine. The second is an article from the Japan-Hawaii Times analyzing American strategic concerns over Hawaii's Japanese population, which Salisbury considers unimportant. The third is a summary of an article by Lieutenant Commander Tota Ishimaru concluding that Japan would almost certainly face defeat if pitted against an Anglo-American coalition and warning Japanese leaders against overestimating their military power.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of ONI Report No. 153 on Translations of War Articles
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A comprehensive ONI report transmitting translations and summaries of War Minister Araki's nationalist pamphlet, an article on Hawaii defense, and a naval strategic study on a Pacific war.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: Report No. 153 provides an unabridged embassy translation of War Minister Sadao Araki's pamphlet promoting the Imperial Way, justifying military action in Manchuria and Mongolia as a moral mission to preserve peace, and discussing the status of Korean settlers in Manchuria and Siberia. The second enclosure summarizes an article by Shoichi A. Asami of the Nippon Jiji (Honolulu) discussing Representative Fred Britten's bill for military government in Hawaii and American fears of Japanese disloyalty. The third enclosure details Lieutenant Commander Tota Ishimaru's analysis of a future Pacific war, examining naval treaty ratios, cruiser and battleship deficiencies, the vital importance of Soviet neutrality, and the severe danger to Japan of an Anglo-American coalition.
subfiles.title: ONI Report No. 153: Translations of War Articles
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum highlighting army setbacks in Manchuria, anti-American propaganda, and Soviet pact overtures reported by the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's dispatch of October 22, 1932, reporting a modest resurgence of conservative influence in Japan. The memorandum highlights the Army's loss of face after failing to clear Manchurian bandits despite expanding its force to 75,000 or 80,000 troops, and describes how an armed robbery in Omori was seized upon to create an anti-communist and anti-American smoke screen. It also notes that War Minister Araki rebuffed Soviet Ambassador Troyanovsky's proposals for a non-aggression pact, citing border unrest at Manzhouli.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of ONI Tokyo Report of October 22, 1932
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An ONI intelligence dispatch covering Japanese reactions to the Lytton Report, military difficulties in Manchuria, political maneuvers involving General Ugaki, and Soviet diplomacy.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The Naval Attach\u00e9 reports that after initial virulent abuse of the Lytton Report, Japanese newspapers adopted a more conciliatory tone, reflecting a resurgence of conservative influence led by Finance Minister Takahashi against War Minister Araki. Rumors circulated that Minseito leaders sought to bring General Kazushige Ugaki from Chosen to head a new cabinet and curb the Young Army faction. In Manchuria, Japanese forces made little headway against insurgents and failed to liberate Japanese hostages held at Manzhouli, leading the military to manufacture a public diversion around an Omori bank heist blamed on communists and American films. Facing strategic impasses, military leaders weighed an arrangement with Chiang Kai-shek against communism, the creation of an autonomous North China regime, or eventual hostilities against Russia while resisting a Soviet non-aggression pact.
subfiles.title: ONI Dispatch: Political Developments, Manchurian Situation, and the Omori Bank Robbery
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department digest of the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's bi-weekly summary covering cabinet politics, the death of Kaku Mori, Yasukuni Shrine disputes, and economic conditions.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury provides a detailed digest of the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's summary of December 16, 1932. Key points include Seiyukai political maneuvering against the Cabinet, fiscal deadlocks between tax increases and military spending, and the passing of Seiyukai power broker Kaku Mori, who had served as the chief liaison between politicians and the Army. The memo notes massive radio traffic between Geneva and Nagoya, the transfer of the naval liaison office to Hsinking, army plans to withdraw instructors from Catholic schools over refusal to bow at Yasukuni Shrine, and public reactions to American Far Eastern policy. Economic and social sections highlight rising commodity prices, banking stress, and police raids arresting 250 suspected communists in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of December 16, 1932
subfiles.to: Eugene H. Dooman / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A bi-weekly intelligence summary reviewing domestic political maneuvers, Shanhaikwan hostilities, Manchurian diplomacy, naval-military changes, and industrial mergers.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The summary examines Seiyukai and Minseito party alignments toward the Cabinet and the political void left by the death of Kaku Mori. It reports on minor clashes at Shanhaikwan, commercial treaty negotiations with Manchukuo, and General Koiso's statements dismissing the need for a Soviet non-aggression pact. Naval and military entries record the sinking of the destroyer Sawarabi, army controversies with Catholic schools over Yasukuni Shrine homage, and Shinsaku Hirata's newspaper critique of unchecked military expenditures. Economic and social developments include falling postal savings, large-scale amalgamations in shipping (NYK, OSK, Kinkai Yusen Kaisha), steel, and paper, unemployment relief bills, and government-directed emigration to Manchukuo.
subfiles.title: ONI Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of December 16, 1932
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A brief State Department memorandum summarizing an ONI report on an air defense blackout drill held in Kobe.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes an ONI report based on an account given by the purser of the S.S. President Lincoln regarding simulated air raid maneuvers in Kobe. The purser observed the rigorous darkening of houses and public enthusiasm during the exercises. The report interprets the heightened public excitement as symptomatic of an underlying popular war sentiment throughout Japan.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of ONI Report on Kobe Air Raid Practice
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An ONI report detailing civilian blackout compliance, street demonstrations, and public enthusiasm during a simulated night air raid in Kobe.
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence (San Francisco Branch)
subfiles.summary: Mr. Kingsbury of the purser's office of the S.S. President Lincoln describes a simulated night air raid conducted in Kobe. Public utility employees went door-to-door distributing blackout cloth and demonstrating light obscuration; when one residence failed to extinguish an exterior gate light, a large crowd demonstrated outside until it was put out. Large crowds filled the streets and cheered loudly when searchlights caught a participating aircraft. The observer considered this public enthusiasm indicative of widespread popular preparedness for war.
subfiles.title: ONI Report: Air Raid Practice at Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's report of January 27, 1933, regarding Diet tranquility, Manchurian campaign costs, Russian whalers, and army swords.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury digests key items from the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's summary of January 27, 1933. The memorandum notes that the Diet opened with unexpected tranquility and cites estimates that operations in Manchuria have cost 573,000,000 yen (nearly 40,000,000 yen monthly) without winning local goodwill. It notes the detention of four Russian whaling vessels in the Bonin Islands on suspicion of espionage and radical agitation, the creation of army-sponsored National Defense Societies in over ten prefectures, and the replacement of Western sabers with traditional two-handed swords in the Japanese Army.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of January 27, 1933
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A comprehensive intelligence summary detailing Diet political maneuvers, Soviet whaler detentions, mandate island defense rumors, naval programs, and May 15 court-martial trials.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The Naval Attach\u00e9 reviews political accommodations in the Diet, where Seiyukai leader Dr. Suzuki avoided confronting the Cabinet after failing to secure military backing. International topics include Soviet protests over Japanese communiqu\u00e9s, the detention of four Russian whaling ships at Futami in the Bonin Islands on espionage charges, and Japanese rebuttals at the League regarding alleged naval fortifications in Palau and Saipan. Naval entries detail Diet debates on the Imperial Command, construction of the destroyer Hatsuharu and river gunboats for Manchukuo, and air base work at Saeki. Economic and social sections report rising foreign trade deficits, bond sales by the Bank of Japan, nationwide petitions for leniency toward officers tried for the May 15 assassinations, labor strife at Osaka Iron Works, and 1930 imperial census statistics.
subfiles.title: ONI Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of January 27, 1933
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum highlighting fleet maneuvers, economic warnings, and colonial communist arrests from the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's January 14, 1933 summary.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury highlights key points of the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's report of January 14, 1933, for Far Eastern Division officers Eugene H. Dooman and M. F. Perkins. The memorandum notes scheduled August naval maneuvers around the Bonin Islands involving all vessels not stationed in China, and warns that Japan's export-driven boom must soon face a severe economic reaction. It also reports large-scale communist plots uncovered in Taiwan and Korea involving hundreds of arrests, and notes government plans to subsidize the emigration of 25,000 Japanese to Brazil.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of January 14, 1933
subfiles.to: Eugene H. Dooman and M. F. Perkins / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An intelligence summary covering Cabinet instability, the Shanhaikwan clash, direct diplomacy versus the League of Nations, naval aviation, and colonial communist crackdowns.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The report examines the Saito Cabinet's weakness, Seiyukai opposition to railway spending cuts, and debates over Navy Minister Admiral Okada's retirement age status. In foreign affairs, Japan pursued direct negotiations while threatening League withdrawal, as fighting erupted at Shanhaikwan and Japanese forces pushed toward Jehol and Pogranichnaya. It details allegations in the Japanese press of American aviation assistance to China, the formation of the Great Asia Association to promote an Asiatic Monroe Doctrine, and justifications for increased military spending. Further sections cover the municipal donation of Ueda airfield in Nagano, the end of search efforts for the sunken destroyer Sawarabi, pending exchange control legislation, suppression of communist conspiracies in Taiwan and Korea, and state-assisted emigration to Brazil.
subfiles.title: ONI Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of January 14, 1933
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's report of December 2, 1932, covering party politics, budget compromises, and social unrest.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury analyzes the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's summary of December 2, 1932, noting it was the first report prepared by Assistant Naval Attach\u00e9 Lieutenant Henri H. Smith-Hutton. The memorandum covers public disillusionment with major parties, cabinet unpopularity, and budget compromises that reduced Army and Navy estimates to 447,000,000 and 372,000,000 yen respectively. It highlights widespread national support for Japan's observations on the Lytton Report, rising military recruitment, plans for military training of 35,000 schoolgirls, and industrial amalgamations in steel and paper. It also records a communist-led peasant uprising in Tottori Prefecture kept secret by police censorship, and clarifies that General Araki did not actually threaten Baron Goh over altering capitalism.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of December 2, 1932
subfiles.to: Eugene H. Dooman and Maxwell M. Hamilton / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An intelligence summary covering party intrigues against the Saito Cabinet, Cabinet approval of the 1933-1934 defense budget, League diplomacy, and industrial amalgamations.
subfiles.from: Lieutenant Henri H. Smith-Hutton / Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Written by Assistant Naval Attach\u00e9 Lieutenant Henri H. Smith-Hutton, this summary assesses party dissatisfaction with the Saito Cabinet, the remote prospects of a Minseito cabinet under General Ugaki, and military dominance over politics. The approved 1933-1934 budget allocates 820,494,000 yen (35 percent of the budget) to the military, financed via public deficit bonds. The report details national excitement over Geneva League proceedings, Japanese rejection of President Hoover's disarmament proposals, and a surge in military and naval academy applicants. Economic and social sections report yen depreciation, the creation of a semi-governmental steel merger centered on Yawata Iron Works, paper company mergers, and significant strikes among seamen and university students.
subfiles.title: ONI Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of December 2, 1932
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum noting an attach\u00e9 report on Japanese Diet interpellations concerning responsibility for determining military strength.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury briefly summarizes an attached ONI report of February 3, 1933, from the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9. The report covers parliamentary interpellations and ministerial replies in the Imperial Diet regarding who bears constitutional responsibility for determining Japan's military strength. Salisbury notes that the substance of this information had already been received in the Far Eastern Division.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of ONI Report on Military Strength Interpellations
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: An intelligence report analyzing Diet debates and the Legislative Bureau's ruling on the constitutional procedure for deciding military strength under the Emperor's Supreme Command.
subfiles.from: Naval Attach\u00e9, Tokyo / Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: The report documents Lower House interpellations by Seiyukai member Shinya Uchida questioning Premier Makoto Saito and War Minister Sadao Araki on whether the government maintained the late Premier Hamaguchi's doctrine regarding naval limitations. In response to apparent contradictions concerning the 'Supreme Command' under Articles XI and XII of the Meiji Constitution, the Premier sought an official ruling from the Director of the Legislative Bureau. The Legislative Bureau ruled that deciding military strength involves defense strategy, diplomacy, finance, and politics, requiring perfect coordination between military command organs and civil administration in counseling the Throne. While accepting the text as an improvement over Hamaguchi's formula, the military authorities demanded assurances that General Staff command decisions would be drawn up independently before being negotiated with the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: ONI Report No. 13: Official Interpretation of the Procedure in Deciding the Military Strength
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence / Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's report of February 24, 1933, on public war fever over the League, naval rumors, and social legislation.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes the Tokyo Naval Attach\u00e9's report of February 24, 1933. The memorandum emphasizes intense public excitement and apprehension over Japan's imminent withdrawal from the League of Nations, along with the Navy Minister's readiness alert to all fleets. It reports Japanese dissatisfaction with the retention of the U.S. Scouting Fleet in the Pacific, rumors of a British offer to make the Singapore naval base available to the U.S. Navy in exchange for war debt relief, and speculation that Yosuke Matsuoka might replace Ambassador Debuchi in Washington. It also notes interest in the commercial exploitation of the Pacific Mandates and a new law legalizing marriages between Japanese and Formosans.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Summary of Bi-Weekly Intelligence Summary of February 24, 1933
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
